name: Papel Picado
basis: why: 'punched paper' banners whose holes are the drawing; how: hole lattice sized by brightness, cut out of the tissue
note: Chisel-punched through stacked tissue, so it could also sit under piercing.

lumenary.blurb: Tissue-paper banners strung across a Mexican street, each one punched with holes. Your picture shows through the openings, which grow wider where the light is strong.

facts.era: Centuries old, with tissue paper from the 19th century
facts.bestOn: Bright, simple pictures with warm colour

why: Papel picado means punched paper. Banners of tissue are strung across streets and altars for fiestas and for the Day of the Dead, and they flutter in the wind, so the light through the holes keeps moving. Holes are the whole drawing here: the more light a place in your picture has, the wider the cut, so the picture shows through the openings.
how: Draw each banner as a rectangle of width w and height 1.18 w, with a zigzag lower edge of seven teeth and a fold at the top where the string runs.
Hang rows from straight lines, shift alternate rows by half a banner and tilt each by a few hundredths of a radian.
Cut by painting in destination-out mode, so cuts remove paper and show what is behind.
Add a border of small holes and a 7 by 7 lattice in the middle, where each hole is sized by the blurred brightness of the picture at that cell.
Colour the tissue from a fiesta, pastel or marigold palette, or from the picture, with a see-through setting.
history: Paper cutting in Mexico has roots in the bark paper (amate) of the Aztecs and in tissue that crossed the Pacific on the Manila galleons from the sixteenth century. The banners are made today by stacking fifty or so sheets and tapping steel chisels through them with a mallet. Papel picado is a symbol of Día de Muertos, on the first and second of November, when it decorates altars for the dead.
uses: Fiesta, wedding and Día de Muertos decoration
terms: Mexican banners of tissue paper cut with patterns.
Bark paper made in Mexico since before the Spanish arrived.
The Day of the Dead, a celebration of remembered family and friends.
paragraphs: Papel picado, “punched paper”, is made by stacking fifty or so sheets of tissue and tapping steel chisels through them with a mallet. The banners are strung across streets and altars for fiestas and for the Day of the Dead. In the program each banner is a rectangle of width w and height 1.18 w with a zigzag lower edge (seven teeth, depth 0.07 h) and a fold at the top where the string runs. Rows of banners hang from straight lines, alternate rows are shifted by half a banner, and each one is tilted by a few hundredths of a radian.

The cuts are made by painting in destination-out mode, so they remove paper and show whatever is behind. A border of small holes runs inside the edge, and the middle is a 7 × 7 lattice of cells. At the centre of each cell the program reads the blurred brightness t of your picture and sets the hole radius from it, so bright places get wide holes and dark places get pin-pricks. The tissue is thin, so a share of the picture is also painted over the paper itself, and a soft shadow falls behind the whole sheet.

equations.note: Hole radius in a lattice cell of side c: t is the picture’s brightness there and h the hole size slider (0.3 to 1). Holes under 0.9 px are skipped.
The fraction of each cell that is open, for round holes. It is how much of the picture shows through.
The tissue is a little see-through: σ is the see-through slider.

presets.text: Pastel tissue on a dusk sky looks like the evening of a festival.
Flower-shaped holes give a floral lace.
Thicker tissue hides more of the backdrop.
